shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · GDP per capita, PPP, current international $ (PPPPC); 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.narration: Eighty-seven percent. {p} In 1995, the average Czech was eighty-seven percent richer than the average Pole, on income adjusted for prices. {pp} This year, in the IMF's numbers, the gap is under seven percent. {p} And by 2031, in the IMF's forecast, it's about four.

On January 1st, 1993, Czechoslovakia split in two. {p} The Czech half was the richer one. {pp} In 1995, Czechia was richer than Slovakia, richer than Slovenia, and far richer than Poland. {p} <soft>So how did Poland close almost the whole gap?</soft>
Quick one before the chart: this is a series about who's passing whom in Europe, and Poland keeps showing up. Subscribe so you don't miss the next one. {p} Now, the head start.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · Czechia's GDP per capita (PPP) as % of Poland's; 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.narration: Here's Czechia as a share of Poland, adjusted for prices. {p} In 1995, a hundred and eighty-seven percent. {pp} Then, in May 1997, a run on the Czech currency. The koruna was set free to float, and the economy shrank two years in a row. {p} From 1996 to 1999, Czechia barely grew at all. Poland grew eighteen percent. {pp} By 2000, the lead was down to fifty-six percent. And there it sat, for almost a decade.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · real GDP growth, Czechia (annual %); 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.narration: Here's Czechia's economy, year by year, after inflation. {p} From 2005 to 2007, a boom: more than five percent a year. {pp} Then the 2008 crisis. In 2009, Czechia shrank four point eight percent. {p} Poland grew two point six. It was the only economy in the European Union that didn't shrink that year. {pp} And Czechia dipped again in 2012.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · real GDP growth (NGDP_RPCH, compounded), population (LP)
shots.title: The crash
shots.narration: Put it together. From 2008 to 2013, after inflation, Czechia's economy shrank about one percent. Poland's grew about fourteen. {p} And over thirty years, from 1995 to 2025, Czechia's economy almost doubled. Poland's roughly tripled. {pp} Czechia has about eleven million people. Poland has more than three times as many.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · GDP per capita, current US$ at market exchange rates (NGDPDPC); 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.narration: Now the twist. In plain dollars, at market exchange rates, Czechia is further ahead. {p} This year, about thirty-nine thousand six hundred dollars a person. Poland, about thirty-one thousand two hundred. {pp} That's about a quarter more. {p} Czechia kept its own currency, and never joined the euro. Neither did Poland. {p} So in plain money, the Czechs are still clearly ahead.
And if you're enjoying the series, the subscribe button is right there. {p} Now, the bigger race.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · GDP per capita, PPP, current international $ (PPPPC); 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.narration: Czechia, Slovenia, Slovakia and Poland. {p} In 2004, adjusted for prices, Slovenia was first and Poland was last. {pp} Since 2009, Czechia has been ahead of Slovenia. And Poland passed Slovakia. {p} So the old Czechoslovakia ended up on both sides of Poland.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · GDP per capita, PPP, current international $ (PPPPC); 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.title: The gap, adjusted for prices
shots.narration: So here's where it stands, in the IMF's numbers. {p} In 2008, Czechia was ahead by about eleven thousand three hundred dollars per person. {p} This year, about four thousand. {pp} And in 2031, in the IMF's forecast, about three thousand one hundred. {p} Czechia is still ahead. But most of that lead is gone.

<soft>So, what's your guess?</soft> {pp} Does Poland pass Czechia in the 2030s, {p} later, {p} or never? {pp} Tell me in the comments. {pp} If you're watching from Czechia: {p} does it feel like this where you are? {pp} I read every comment.
And if you missed it, {p} this is the one where Slovenia was seventy-one percent richer, and now it's almost even. {pp} It's right here. {pp} I'm Chartbound. {p} See you in the next one.

checks.say: 1995: CZE > SVK, SVN; CZE far richer than POL
growth 1997, 1998 < 0 (shrank two years in a row); 1996→1999 CZE ~0%, POL +18%
USD 2026: CZE ≈ 39,600, POL ≈ 31,200; ratio ≈ 1.27 (about a quarter more); USD ratio > PPP ratio (further ahead)
2004 order SVN > CZE > SVK > POL; CZE > SVN every year 2009–2031; POL > SVK 2026

yt.title: Czechia Was 87% Richer Than Poland. Now It's Just 7%.
yt.description:
Income per person adjusted for prices (IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026): in 1995 the average Czech was 87% ahead of the average Pole. This year the gap is under 7%, and in the IMF's 2031 forecast it's about 4%. The May 1997 currency crisis, the 2009 crash (−4.8% while Poland grew 2.6%), why Czechia is still about a quarter richer in plain dollars, and how the old Czechoslovakia ended up on both sides of Poland.

Sources: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 (PPPPC, NGDPDPC, NGDP_RPCH, LP). 2026+ figures are IMF estimates and forecasts.
